title: bug: Safety is violated
body:
In the presence of an attacker or a twin, replicas can commit different blocks on different branches.

This is shown by the `TestSafetyWithTwins` test on `TwinsIssue` branch.
The issue is probably due to a wrong implementation of the commit rule for chaines hotstuff. 
The commit rule was implemented verbatim from the hotstuff paper. 
However, the paper assumes that dummy blocks are inserted for every view, such that the view of the parent always is the current view-1.
However, our implementation does not use dummy blocks. Instead, normally the parent's view is the same as the view in the QC.

title: Bug: Panic when receiving QC for non-existent block (Ghost QC Attack)
body:
### Description

The system panics when processing a QC that points to a non-existent block (ghost block). This is a critical DoS vulnerability - an attacker can crash any node by sending a validly-signed QC pointing to a random hash.

### Root Cause

1. `VerifyQuorumCert()` in `security/cert/auth.go` calls `blockchain.Get()` to fetch the block
2. `blockchain.Get()` attempts network fetch when block not found locally
3. This calls `eventLoop.TimeoutContext()` which calls `context.WithCancel(el.Context())`
4. If `el.Context()` returns nil, `context.WithCancel(nil)` panics

### Attack Vector

```
Attacker sends: NewViewMsg { QC: { BlockHash: <random>, Signatures: <valid> } }
→ Node receives QC
→ VerifyQuorumCert() called
→ blockchain.Get(<random_hash>)
→ eventLoop.TimeoutContext()
→ context.WithCancel(nil)
→ PANIC!
```

### Impact

- **Severity**: Critical (DoS)
- **Attack Cost**: Low (only requires forging QC signatures)
- **Affected**: All nodes in the network

### Fix

1. Use `LocalGet()` instead of `Get()` in `VerifyQuorumCert` and `VerifyPartialCert`
2. Add nil context fallback in `ViewContext()` for robustness

title: bug: Failure to create quorum certificates with dublicate signers
body:
The voting machine does not filter duplicate votes, i.e., receiving the same vote message twice. 
However, `CreateQuorumCert` checks for duplicates and returns an `ErrCombineOverlap`.

This is a serious issue since it allows a faulty replica to undermine liveness. 
If the replica sends duplicate votes, no quorum certificate can be formed.

To reproduce the error, run the `TestBasicTwinsScenario` test on the `twinsissue` branch.

Safety & Liveness Vulnerability in AggregateQC Creation and Verification
body:
Hello, I am currently using this project to implement a new HotStuff-family consensus algorithm based on my theoretical work. During the implementation of a new synchronizer, I came across a potential vulnerability that could severely impact liveness, which I've detailed below.

My main question is whether this behavior is intentional. I am wondering if this was a known trade-off for a research-focused implementation or a possible oversight. This is important for my own work, as I am currently deciding whether to address this potential attack vector in my implementation before proceeding with benchmarks. Any clarification would be greatly appreciated

### Description
A critical safety and liveness vulnerability has been identified in the CreateAggregateQC and VerifyAggregateQC functions within crypto.go. The current implementation is susceptible to a denial-of-service (DoS) attack orchestrated by a single Byzantine node, which can indefinitely stall the consensus process.

### The Problem
The CreateAggregateQC function collects Quorum Certificates (QCs) from TimeoutMsg payloads sent by replicas without individually verifying each QC's validity. It blindly trusts the received QCs and includes them in the resulting AggregateQC.

Subsequently, the VerifyAggregateQC function identifies the QC with the highest view number (highQC) from the collected set and performs a verification check only on this highQC.

This creates a single point of failure. A Byzantine replica can craft a TimeoutMsg containing a forged QC with a deceptively high view number. When the leader creates the AggregateQC, this invalid highQC will be included. When other honest replicas attempt to verify this AggregateQC, the c.VerifyQuorumCert(highQC) check will fail, causing the entire AggregateQC to be rejected.

This allows a single malicious actor to repeatedly invalidate AggregateQCs, preventing the consensus from advancing.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. A Byzantine replica sends a TimeoutMsg to the current leader.
2. This message contains a forged QuorumCert with a view number higher than any valid QC held by other replicas.
3. The leader calls CreateAggregateQC, which trustingly includes the forged QC in a new AggregateQC.
4. The leader proposes this AggregateQC to the network.
5. Honest replicas receive the AggregateQC and call VerifyAggregateQC.
6. The verification fails because the embedded highQC (the forged one) is invalid.
7. The consensus process stalls as no valid AggregateQC can be formed.

### Impact
A single Byzantine node can perpetually halt the consensus mechanism, leading to a complete stall of the blockchain.

### Recommendation
To mitigate this vulnerability, it is crucial to verify each individual QC before it is included in the AggregateQC.

The CreateAggregateQC function should be modified to iterate through all incoming TimeoutMsgs and validate their contained QCs using VerifyQuorumCert. Only QCs that pass this verification should be added to the qcs map.

body:
We should remove the `highQC` argument from the `ProposeRule` interface's signature. The argument is unnecessary since the `cert` (`SyncInfo`) argument contains the same QC as the provided `highQC`.

It is the `Proposer`'s `CreateProposal` method that calls the concrete `ProposeRule` implementations. The basic logic looks like this:
```go
func (p *Proposer) CreateProposal(syncInfo hotstuff.SyncInfo) (proposal hotstuff.ProposeMsg, err error) {
...
	highQC := p.states.HighQC()
...
	proposal, ok := p.ruler.ProposeRule(view, highQC, syncInfo, cmdBatch)
...
```

The `CreateProposal` is called from `Synchronizer.Start()`:
```go
		syncInfo := s.state.SyncInfo()
		proposal, err := s.proposer.CreateProposal(syncInfo)
```
Here, `s.state.SyncInfo()` essentially gets the same `highQC` as the `p.states.HighQC()` (there is only one instance of `ViewStates`).

The `CreateProposal` is also called from `Synchronizer.advanceView(syncInfo)`:
```go
func (s *Synchronizer) advanceView(syncInfo hotstuff.SyncInfo) {
...
	qc, view, timeout, err := s.timeoutRules.VerifySyncInfo(syncInfo)
...
	if qc != nil {

	if leader == s.config.ID() {

...
```

title: --list-modules CLI flag produces segfault
body:
The `--list-modules` CLI flag produces a segfault:

```
› make && ./hotstuff --list-modules
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0xe8 pc=0x70ca1c]

goroutine 1 [running]:
github.com/relab/hotstuff/modules.ListModules()
	/home/michael/dev/go/hotstuff/modules/registry.go:89 +0x1dc
github.com/relab/hotstuff/internal/cli.glob..func1(0x11be760?, {0xc1f2a6?, 0x1?, 0x1?})
	/home/michael/dev/go/hotstuff/internal/cli/root.go:37 +0x34
github.com/spf13/cobra.(*Command).execute(0x11be760, {0xc0001a8010, 0x1, 0x1})
	/home/michael/go/pkg/mod/github.com/spf13/cobra@v1.4.0/command.go:856 +0x67c
github.com/spf13/cobra.(*Command).ExecuteC(0x11be760)
	/home/michael/go/pkg/mod/github.com/spf13/cobra@v1.4.0/command.go:974 +0x3bd
github.com/spf13/cobra.(*Command).Execute(...)
	/home/michael/go/pkg/mod/github.com/spf13/cobra@v1.4.0/command.go:902
github.com/relab/hotstuff/internal/cli.Execute()
	/home/michael/dev/go/hotstuff/internal/cli/root.go:52 +0x25
main.main()
	/home/michael/dev/go/hotstuff/cmd/hotstuff/main.go:7 +0x17
```
Following the stack trace shows it must be due to the `t` variable, a key of the `byInterface` map, being `<nil>`: https://github.com/relab/hotstuff/blob/master/modules/registry.go#L89

The queried datastructure (`byInterface`) is only filled within here, where the offending map key is called `moduleType`: https://github.com/relab/hotstuff/blob/master/modules/registry.go#L31-L34

`moduleType` is set in the same function as `moduleType := reflect.TypeOf(t)`. Here, `var t T` is (the zero value of) a variable of type `T`. `T` is seemingly the (generic) return type of the constructor of the module which is being registered.

Which brings us to the likely cause. The return type of at least some of the registered modules' constructors is an interface, e.g here: https://github.com/relab/hotstuff/blob/master/consensus/byzantine/byzantine.go#L11

Thus `var t T` has the zero value of an interface, which is `<nil>`. `moduleType := reflect.TypeOf(t)` [returns `nil` as `t` is a `nil` interface](https://pkg.go.dev/reflect#TypeOf). This ends up in the `byInterface` map. And eventually it blows up when one tries to access it as something of type `reflect.Type`.

I don't understand why you seemingly keep modules grouped by their constructor's return value in the `byInterface` data structure, and why you want to print them that way in the `--list-modules` call, so am hesitant to recommend a fix.

title: Consensus impl question
Liveness Regression: Lagging Nodes Cannot Sync After LocalGet Change
body:
## Background

PR #285 fixed a critical DoS vulnerability by changing `VerifyQuorumCert` to use `LocalGet()` instead of `Get()`. This prevents attackers from triggering expensive network requests by sending QCs referencing non-existent blocks.

## Problem

However, this change introduced a **liveness regression**: legitimate lagging nodes can no longer sync up with the cluster.

## Root Cause Analysis

When `VerifyQuorumCert` uses `LocalGet()`:

1. A lagging node receives a `NewViewMsg` or `ProposeMsg` with a high-view QC
2. The QC references a block the node doesn't have locally
3. `LocalGet()` returns "block not found"
4. `VerifySyncInfo` fails, `advanceView` returns early
5. **No Fetch mechanism is triggered**
6. The node remains stuck at its old view **forever**

## Evidence

Static analysis shows the error handling in `advanceView`:

```go
qc, view, timeout, err := s.timeoutRules.VerifySyncInfo(syncInfo)
if err != nil {
    s.logger.Infof("advanceView: Failed to verify sync info: %v", err)
    return  // Message dropped, no sync triggered!
}
```

Regression test results confirm:
- Nodes 1-3: 47 commits each
- Node 4 (isolated for 10 views): **0 commits** after rejoining

## Impact

- **Severity**: High
- Any node that loses connectivity temporarily will be permanently stuck
- Network partitions become unrecoverable without manual intervention

## Proposed Solution

Add controlled block prefetching in `advanceView` before QC verification:

```go
if qc, ok := syncInfo.QC(); ok {
    s.state.FetchBlock(qc.BlockHash())  // Fetch if missing
}
// Then verify with LocalGet (safe, block now available)
```

This maintains DoS protection (only fetches for legitimate protocol messages) while restoring liveness.

title: Module system inconsistencies
body:
The module system is powerful but has some inconsistencies:

- Some modules, such as `consensus.Rules`, are initialized inside another module, `consensus.Consensus`, and not added to the builder. 
- Most structs that implement `modules.Module` only have one implementation and are not modular.

Edit: Further issues:
- Circular dependencies causes the need for dependency injection, which is not idiomatic go code. Solving cyclic imports without dependency injection and refactoring modules could simplify the module system greatly to the point where a builder is not even needed.

body: Hello Sui Team, I have isolated a critical bug in the Mysten Labs Move extension on macOS. The issue is not a gradual memory leak over time, but an immediate and severe problem that occurs the moment the extension is activated. I have confirmed that **this issue is caused specifically by the Mysten Labs Move extension.** If I disable or uninstall this extension, the problem disappears completely and system stability is restored. **Problem Summary** When a VSCode window containing `.move` files is opened, the Move extension activates and launches the `move-analyzer` process. This immediately triggers two critical failures: 1. **Immediate Memory Leak:** The `move-analyzer` process starts consuming excessive amounts of memory right away, quickly leading to system slowdown. 2. **Guaranteed Orphaned Process:** After quitting VSCode, the `move-analyzer` process is **never** terminated. It remains as a zombie process, holding onto all the leaked memory. **Steps to Reproduce** 1. Ensure the "Move Language Extension for Sui (Mysten Labs)" is installed and enabled in VSCode. 2. Open a VSCode window with a project workspace that includes any `.move` files. (It is not necessary to open the file itself; just having it in the workspace triggers the extension). 3. Immediately open the macOS Activity Monitor. 4. Observe the `move-analyzer` process rapidly consuming memory. 5. Completely quit VSCode (using `Cmd+Q`). 6. Observe in the Activity Monitor that the `move-analyzer` process is still running. 7. **(Verification Step)** Disable the Move extension, restart VSCode, and open the same project. title: sui-types: A potential double-lock bug in storage
body:
## Steps to Reproduce Issue

There is a potential double-lock bug in sui-types found by chain-fox.

For more details, please refer to [chain-fox.com/reports](https://www.chain-fox.com/reports).
We develop tools that automatically detect bugs commonly overlooked by developers and human auditors.
If you find our tools helpful, we are also looking for a long-term partnership to continue uncovering bugs together.

The following is a brief introduction:

https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/f85fa757f827f62301561cd8b32e0a85d902b828/crates/sui-types/src/storage/shared_in_memory_store.rs#L21-L32
`SharedInMemoryStore` contains an RwLock, `inner()` calls read lock on it, and `inner_mut()` calls write lock on it.

https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/f85fa757f827f62301561cd8b32e0a85d902b828/crates/sui-types/src/storage/shared_in_memory_store.rs#L74-L86

The first read lock is acquired on L72.
Then from_checkpoint_contents is called on L84
Next store.get_transaction and store.get_transaction_effects are called in the following code:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/f85fa757f827f62301561cd8b32e0a85d902b828/crates/sui-types/src/messages_checkpoint.rs#L593-L594
Then get_transaction and get_transaction_effects are called in the following code:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/f85fa757f827f62301561cd8b32e0a85d902b828/crates/sui-types/src/storage/read_store.rs#L282
https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/f85fa757f827f62301561cd8b32e0a85d902b828/crates/sui-types/src/storage/read_store.rs#L282
Finally, the second lock is acquired on L96 or L102
https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/f85fa757f827f62301561cd8b32e0a85d902b828/crates/sui-types/src/storage/shared_in_memory_store.rs#L95-L103


## Expected Result

No deadlock should occur.

## Actual Result

Recent optimizations to RwLock in std::sync have changed the behavior of recursive read locks on Linux.
It will cause the following code to deadlock on Linux.

https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&gist=4a1463bd66bc6914d7ffc6ea8b8f1ac6

https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.RwLock.html warns of this kind of deadlock.

Basically, the write lock has a higher priority than the read lock. When trying to acquire a write lock in between two recursive read locks, the second read lock cannot be acquired, which in turn prevents the release of the first read lock.


## System Information

* OS: Linux
* Compiler: rustc nightly

title: [zksend] 0.12.1 bugs
Sui Code Bug in Typescript SDK
body:
## Steps to Reproduce Issue

1. Install the sdk `npm i @mysten/sui.js`
2. Create a file `test.js` with the following contents:
```
import { getFullnodeUrl, SuiClient } from '@mysten/sui.js/client';
 
// use getFullnodeUrl to define Devnet RPC location
const rpcUrl = getFullnodeUrl('mainnet');
 
// create a client connected to devnet
const client = new SuiClient({ url: rpcUrl });
 
// get coins owned by an address
// replace <OWNER_ADDRESS> with actual address in the form of 0x123...
await client.getCoins({
	owner: '0xb29c543ed7ad7169441c02fc14ffd57e486b7be7177e319de0e0933453a78d49',
});
```
3. Run the code with `node test.js`

## Expected Result

Code runs.


## Actual Result

Code crashes with the following
```
file:///home/dev/project/node_modules/@mysten/sui.js/dist/esm/client/http-transport.js:38
      throw new Error(
            ^

Error: The current environment does not support fetch, you can provide a fetch implementation in the options for SuiHTTPTransport.
    at SuiHTTPTransport.fetch (file:///home/dev/project/node_modules/@mysten/sui.js/dist/esm/client/http-transport.js:38:13)
    at SuiHTTPTransport.request (file:///home/dev/project/node_modules/@mysten/sui.js/dist/esm/client/http-transport.js:46:28)
    at SuiClient.getCoins (file:///home/dev/project/node_modules/@mysten/sui.js/dist/esm/client/client.js:42:33)
    at file:///home/dev/project/src/testSuiClient.js:11:14
    at ModuleJob.run (node:internal/modules/esm/module_job:197:25)
    at async Promise.all (index 0)
    at async ESMLoader.import (node:internal/modules/esm/loader:337:24)
    at async loadESM (node:internal/process/esm_loader:88:5)
    at async handleMainPromise (node:internal/modules/run_main:61:12)
```

## System Information

* OS: Linux, ubuntu
* Package version: "@mysten/sui.js": "^0.54.1",


It appears that the default configuration of the sdk is using `fetch`, but not importing `node-fetch` or another implementation.
To fix this, I followed [this ](https://github.com/node-fetch/node-fetch?tab=readme-ov-file#providing-global-access)

I installed `node-fetch` and added the following to the top of my script:
```
// fetch-polyfill.js
import fetch, {
  Blob,
  blobFrom,
  blobFromSync,
  File,
  fileFrom,
  fileFromSync,
  FormData,
  Headers,
  Request,
  Response,
} from 'node-fetch'

if (!globalThis.fetch) {
  globalThis.fetch = fetch
  globalThis.Headers = Headers
  globalThis.Request = Request
  globalThis.Response = Response
}

// index.js
import './fetch-polyfill'

// ...
```

Perhaps this should be documented, or the SDK should import `node-fetch` explicitly before using it.
This may be affecting other packages as well.
I ran into this issue when using the cetus sdk, see issue [here ](https://github.com/CetusProtocol/cetus-clmm-sui-sdk/issues/6)

title: fix(consensus): Missing authority index bounds checking causes DoS vulnerability
body:
## Summary

A Byzantine validator can crash honest validators by sending blocks with invalid authority indices, causing index-out-of-bounds panics.

## Problem Description

When processing blocks from other validators, the consensus layer accesses arrays using authority indices without bounds checking. A malicious validator can craft a block with an invalid author index (e.g., 255 when committee size is 4), causing honest validators to panic when they try to access arrays at these invalid indices.

### Affected Code Paths

- `DagState::contains_blocks()` - panics when checking if block with invalid author exists
- `DagState::get_cached_blocks_in_range()` - panics on `recent_refs_by_authority[authority]` access
- `DagState::get_last_cached_block_in_range()` - panics on array access
- `DagState::contains_cached_block_at_slot()` - panics on `evicted_rounds[slot.authority]` access
- `BlockManager::update_block_received_metrics()` - panics on `received_block_rounds[block.author()]` access

### Attack Scenario

1. Malicious validator crafts a block with `author = AuthorityIndex(255)`
2. Honest validator receives this block and tries to process it
3. Code accesses `recent_refs_by_authority[255]` where array size is only 4
4. Index out of bounds panic crashes the honest validator
5. Single Byzantine validator can crash all honest validators (DoS)

## Proposed Solution

Add defensive bounds checking before all array accesses using authority index:
- Add `is_valid_authority()` helper to DagState for bounds validation
- Add `get_hostname()` helper to BlockManager with fallback for invalid indices
- Return empty/false/None for invalid indices instead of panicking
- Log warnings for defense in depth monitoring

## Security Impact

- **Severity**: High (DoS vulnerability)
- **Attack Vector**: Network (Byzantine validator)
- **Impact**: All honest validators can be crashed by a single malicious validator

title: Execution of sequenced shared object certs may race, leading to unnecessary errors
body:
Here's the situation:

- Suppose consensus adapter has timed out for some number of certs, but those certs have actually made it into consensus.
- A validator will then receive those certs from consensus, sequence them, and put them into the execution driver queue.
- Execution driver wakes up, and attempts to execute all certs in its queue by sending them to NodeSyncState.
- The pending queue is ordered by insert time, so it is guaranteed to preserve the ordering of certs as they arrived from consensus (assuming that none of those certs arrived via some other channel in the meantime).
- However, NodeSyncState parallelizes cert execution, and it is unaware of dependencies among its inputs. Given certs A and B which are sequenced in the order A, B, even though we send A to NodeSyncState first, it will race with B, and B may fail before A is finished, even though it would have completed successfully if A had been executed first.
- This leads to NodeSyncState deciding that parent certs are missing, which causes it to ask other validators to provide it with the cert's effects. Those other validators may be in the same situation.

Some additional observations:

- If a cert was enqueued for execution by the consensus task, then all the shared object dependencies of that cert must have been enqueued previously. If this was the only way that certs were enqueued, then we could be assured that all shared object parents of a cert in the queue must precede it in the queue, or have been previously executed.
- However, certs may also be enqueued by gossip which doesn't provide this guarantee. (Although gossip transmits digests in causal order, validators randomly shuffle their gossip peers, and so may receive a cert via gossip without first receiving that certs parents).
- Additionally, a shared object cert that arrives via consensus may have missing owned object parent certs (e.g. for the gas object), which themselves do not have any shared inputs, and hence will not have arrived via consensus. While the 2f+1 signers of the cert must have executed the missing parent certs, they may not yet be able to execute the cert itself if they have not sequenced it, hence they will not be able to provide TransactionEffects, which is how we normally obtain parent information.
- Because of the above, and also because parallel execution of the pending list will be required to achieve desired throughput, we should treat the execution driver queue as unordered. It's not reliable, and even if it were, it would not be useful since we can't serialize execution of the whole queue.

Proposed solution:

While the execution driver / NodeSyncState lacks explicit parent information (because it does not have TransactionEffects), we can compute a partial ordering of the certs in the queue, as follows:
- Two certs with a shared input in common can be ordered based on the local shared locks. If shared locks are missing the cert is not executable anyway.

```

```

The failure originates here: https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/89d214153df4898e630f107787e1bb5a55794ad6/narwhal/worker/src/worker.rs#L528

I modified the code to not panic immediately on failure, and instead wait, and found that the port is released shortly (_very shortly_) after the failed bind:

```
2022-01-03T02:05:01.237268Z DEBUG node{id=2 name="k#99f25ef6.."}: msim::sim::net::network: /build/.cargo/git/checkouts/mysten-sim-6c6e892b5d19dc47/030cd30/msim/src/sim/net/network.rs:156: binding: 0.0.0.0:4000 -> Node(2)
2022-01-03T02:05:01.237268Z  WARN node{id=2 name="k#99f25ef6.."}: msim::sim::net::network: /build/.cargo/git/checkouts/mysten-sim-6c6e892b5d19dc47/030cd30/msim/src/sim/net/network.rs:188: bind() error: address already in use: 10.10.0.1:4000
2022-01-03T02:05:01.237277Z DEBUG node{id=2 name="k#99f25ef6.."}: msim::sim::net::network: /build/.cargo/git/checkouts/mysten-sim-6c6e892b5d19dc47/030cd30/msim/src/sim/net/network.rs:269: close: Node(2) 10.10.0.1:4000

title: [safety] rate limit peers for pending header parents
body:
### Description

From the issue MystenLabs/narwhal#78 

> We discussed with @asonnino offline about the liveness lock concerns and it seems that we might want to tackle this problem in a different manner to ensure we don't break liveness assumptions that research guarantees. On high level, an adversary that can slow down an honest node which implements the proposed fix, can bring the honest node to a point that will stop operating (acknowledging headers) and basically break the liveness assumptions and make our system susceptible to attacks.
> 
> Instead, we reduced the problem to receiving headers for which we don't manage to get their parents certificates (because the header is basically junk). Keep receiving such headers can lead to getting swamped by messages from potentially dishonest nodes and practically slow down our node. In this case we might want to throttle the peer node and ensure that we put a cap on the number of pending headers (for which we don't have their partner certificates). So if the received headers are junk (very high round number without 2f+1 parents) , we'll eventually stop receiving headers from that peer node until the buffer is cleaned up (this won't affect our ability to receive and process headers from rest of peers). We can probably have mechanisms to eventually clean up / GC those buffers as well. The upside of this method is that we don't break liveness guarantees only because we observe headers with high round numbers (which could be our node catching up) and we limit suspicious activity. If the peer node is honest and we happen to eventually receive those certificates, the buffer will get cleared up and we'll continue processing headers from that node again.

As part of this task we want to introduce the above mechanism to rate limit (throttle) peers when receiving headers for processing for which we are waiting to receive their certificate parents. We want the rate limiting to be independent for each peer and not affect one each other. For example, at the moment if we receive a header from a peer node `A` for processing, and their parents are missing from our internal storage, we first request the parents and then we proceed with the processing. We want to implement a mechanism like a bounded queue or similar, which will represent the maximum number of headers that we can have pending for processing for a specific peer (example `A`) . If the queue has reached its capacity, the we stop processing headers from them until we resolve the references for the existing/pending ones.

Note: based on the GC strategy, it seems that some sort of cleanup is [already happening on the `certificate_waiter`](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/c13f52217343f5f936b0dfa22680fe413332b6dc/primary/src/certificate_waiter.rs#L122) . So eventually GC will clean up any old requests waiting for parent certificates - irrespective of the node.

title: Unit/integration tests for restart safety
body:
We need to introduce unit/integration tests that run as part of our normal CI test flow that confirms when we shutdown a node (primary/worker) then all its internals components are properly shutdown and nothing runs in detached mode.

More specifically we need to at least ensure we:

* shutdown (and wait until succeeds) every spawned task
* released any holds to the rocks db
* networking has properly shutdown (all the interfaces)



Ultimately on our testing we should confirm at minimum that when we bring down a node and spin up again with:

* same database path
* same networking addresses

there is no conflict and nodes are able to successfully bootstrap

title: Able to add multiple prometheus Registries in SUI
body:
In order to successfully bring down a primary/worker node and bring it up again we need to ensure that metrics will work as expected. Right now when a node is bootstrapped we pass in the prometheus Registry created from SUI and we register the node’s metrics. However, if we are going to restart the node then the same metrics will be attempted to get registered and that will lead to an error. To by pass this issue there are (at least) two approaches we can take:

# Unregister each node’s metrics after we bring down the nodes
# Modify the current SUI code to allow us create multiple prometheus registries - so instead of unregistering metrics we can just provide a fresh new registry and ensure no collisions will exist

Both approaches have their prons/cons but probably the (2) is the most straightforward one in terms of any inherent risks by accidentally forgetting to unregister metrics + the accounting behind it.

*Technical Approach*

* modify the {{start_prometheus_server}} in SUI. It can still create a registry (which can be considered the “main” registry for the app) , but also return another handler that can be shared across the codebase to create new/remove registries
* the above handler should bear some concurrency semantics so we can safely update the current registries
* whenever we want to create a new Registry (ex to pass as part of epoch change to a new spin up primary) , we are creating it and call an {{add}} method to add it to the handler. The handler also ensures that the registry will become available for querying later on. For extra safety , whenever we are adding a new registry we can iterate over the metrics and check against the other registries whether metric with same {{name}} and {{description}} exist - if yes then we can panic as this should not happen
* a {{remove}} method should be created to remove an already registered metric - that would be useful for example after we have shutdown a Narwhal node and we no longer need the defined metrics on its registry
* the {{metrics}} endpoint should be modified to query now multiple registries, merge the results and serve them back.

title: [network] The BoundedExecutor-per-destinary can cause network starvation
body:
### Context
MystenLabs/narwhal#559 incidentally introduced (in the Primary and Worker networks, code pointers hereafter in the primary) one bounded executor per destinary, rather than one global `BoundedExecutor`:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/282e4f8c5856da96d2fbf9a86a997dc68d8a77d7/network/src/primary.rs#L116-L117

The unhappy case of this `BoundedExecutor` (when the executor runs out of tickets) makes the `send_message` functions of our network blocking:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/main/network/src/bounded_executor.rs#L89

### The issue (credits @andll for the find!)

Filling up the `BoundedExecutor` tickets for one specific validator will make the `send_message` operation blocking. If this blocking operation exists in a code path which is shared with other validators, the code path will be blocked for all validators (head-of-line blocking).

One such code path can be found, for example, in the helper, where a `PayloadAvailabilityRequest` or `CertificatesRequest` both lead to an `unreliable_send_message`:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/282e4f8c5856da96d2fbf9a86a997dc68d8a77d7/primary/src/helper.rs#L86-L113

We suspect we've seen this experimentally (with a sharp increase in occupancy of `tx_helper_requests`).

## The Fix

1. for the `UnreliableNetwork` : we can drop the messages destined to an overloaded peer on the floor, specifically because these messages are determined to be strictly needed for the progress of the protocol.
A mitigation is available at https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/commit/219cc82b35293576b4be7abcd706f4b5e81e4eb1 in that direction,
2. for the `ReliableNetwork`: we can expose `spawn_with_permit` and preemptively acquire a permit for sending a message before going into a `tokio::select` branch that requires the ability to send in a non-blocking fashion. The tooling to do that was introduced in MystenLabs/narwhal#724

title: Support sponsored transactions
body:
# Feature Request: Sponsored transactions
Support a transaction type where `TxContext::sender()` is address `A`, but the the gas object that pays for the transaction belongs to address `B`. Such a tx will be first signed by `A`, and then signed again by `B`.

This feature is sometimes called "meta-transactions" or [gasless transactions](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/learn/sending-gasless-transactions) on other platforms. We use the term "sponsored" because our sponsored transactions are ordinary (not meta), and someone still pays for the gas, so "gasless" doesn't quite fit.

## Motivation

The requirement to acquire tokens before sending transactions is a huge pain point. Users need to sign up at exchange, KYC, connect debit card, go through a waiting period before using tokens, … In addition, entities that want to manage keys for their users must become custodians (a very stringent process) because every account that wants to take action needs tokens.

Sponsored transactions alleviate this by decoupling sending transactions and holding tokens. This also helps in non-omnibus custodial settings (e.g., a custodial game server w/ separate Sui accounts for each user). Without sponsored transactions, the game server would have to carefully (and frequently) send txes to top up the gas coins in each player account so it can subsequently sign/send transactions on behalf of the player. But with them, it can hold all the gas in an admin account (or a few admin accounts).

## Comparison to other platforms

This feature exists on other platforms, but we can implement this feature generically, which will be significantly simpler for end-users and programmers, and also more cost-effective.
- In Eth, meta-transactions aren't part of the protocol. A contract has to explicitly "opt-in" to supporting meta-transactions by implementing [EIP2771](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2771). If it doesn't, you have use normal transactions.
- A user that wants to send a meta-transaction has to choose a [forwarder](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/metatx/MinimalForwarder.sol) contract implementation to use. This contract accepts transactions sends by the gas payer, then interprets the calldata as a transaction sent by the user (reflection!), hence the name "meta-transaction" (whereas our implementation is more direct--no reflection or meta-step).
- This is a lot more expensive than sending an ordinary transaction, and potentially scary because you have to trust the forwarder, which is a third-party contract.
- In Sui, there's no need for a programmer to "opt in" to supporting gasless transactions--it won't even be possible to tell the difference between a gasless tx and a normal tx from inside Move.
- In Sui, there's no need for a forwarder.
- In Sui, gasless txes should probably cost a bit more than ordinary ones (will include one extra signature, address, and pubkey, and do one extra signature check), but hop

title: [fastx dist sys] Design and implement re-configuration
body:
fastx operates in epochs. Within each epoch committee and stake are stable, but between epochs they may change. Between epoch a rec-configuration protocol is ran between validators and a consensus system to ensure safety and liveness. We need to implement this re-configuration mechanism, specifically:
- The logic by which a validator closes an epoch, and asks 2f+1 validators of the next epoch to provide a certificate over the set of certificates processed.
- The logic by which an epoch starts through a validator accepting the first 2f+1 certificates (on the consensus core), initializes its database, and start processing transactions.
- Efficiency improvements to minimize downtime.
- Make decisions and implement the smart contract on an L1/consensus core driving the governance logic, and sequencing the certificates of state between epochs.

The current handler for `handle_commit` does two separate writes to the database, one to write the certificate, and another to update the locks. An unfortunate crash between these two calls, will leave the DB in an potentially inconsistent state (maybe?)
https://github.com/MystenLabs/fastnft/blob/48dbe196905eb6c4b3d25669ef5e73d956b753bc/sui_core/src/authority.rs#L490-L495

Either we need to convince ourselves that such a crash will not lead to any unsafety, and write a small essay at this location to remember why, or we should create a call that does a batch write in the DB where all the state is updated or none is.

title: [shared-objects] Client - Consensus Interface
body:
What is the best way to allow clients to communicate with consensus?

### The story so far
Right now clients communicate with the core by sending transactions and certificates (forgetting non-safety critical sync messages).

### What has to change
Clients still send transactions to the core. But to support shared objects, clients now have two options when sending their certificates: (i) either they send it to the core for normal processing, or (ii) they first send it to consensus *and then* send it to the core for normal processing. Option (i) is selected when there are no shared-objects involved in the transaction, and option (ii) is required when the transaction contains a shared object.

title: Relax the 'store' requirement for sui::dynamic_field::add, but enforce the same rules as polymorphic-transfer
body:
Currently, NFT standards are trying to restrict the ability to transfer ownership of objects; not all creators will want their objects to be transferrable, or they will want their own custom transfer function.

(”Transfer” simply changes the Sui-defined owner from 0x123 -> 0x789.)

Any object with key + store can be transferred arbitrarily, using sui::transfer::transfer (polymorphic transfer). This is because if an object can be stored, you could create a custom object, store it, transfer it, and then unwrap it. Also, an object must have ‘key’ so it can be stored at the root-level of global storage using its UID (otherwise there is nothing to ‘transfer’).

Child objects (dynamic object fields) are currently required to have key + store.

The ‘store’ requirement could be relaxed, because the dynamic field is only storing an object-id, not the object itself. However, removing ‘store’ as a requirement alone would be a bad idea; in that case, any object with ‘key’ could be made a child object of an object with key + store; the parent object would then be transferred, the child object removed; we'd be back at polymorphic transfer again.

As such, I think rather than having sui::dynamic_field::add() as being the function people use to add a child to a parent, we should instead go back to using sui::transfer::transfer_to_object() (we can keep using sui::dynamic_field::add() if you prefer):

transfer_to_object will have the same restrictions that transfer::transfer does:

- It can be used universally on any object with key + store
- It can be used on any object with key, but only within the module that defines the object

Hence, creators can create an NFT that only has ‘key’ ability, and then can define their own custom logic by which that NFT can be (1) transferred to another person (transfer::transfer) or (2) transferred to another object (transfer::transfer_to_object()).

This won’t affect bag and table, because bag and table are restricted to only key + store objects anyway, and don't need permission from the defining module in order to transfer them in any way.

This will allow NFTs that cannot be polymorphic-transferred to still be used as children of parent objects (with the defining module's permission).

title: [fastx types] make size of Move's `address` type configurable
body:
Move account addresses are 16 bytes. We would like to make them the same size as fastX authenticators (i.e., `FastPayAddress`), and (ideally) fastX `ObjectID`'s too. We haven't decided on the size of either of those types yet, but they will likely need to be >= 20 bytes for safety (e.g., a 32 byte hash truncated to the shortest length that is safe w.r.t collisions). 

Whatever length(s) we chose, we need to be able to adjust Move addresses accordingly. The size of Move addresses is determined by [this](https://github.com/diem/diem/blob/main/language/move-core/types/src/account_address.rs#L20) constant in the Diem codebase. We need to tweak it via one mechanism or another. Some ideas:
- `cargo` magic to set a constant at compile-time via a build config (preferred long-term solution)
- Use `cargo`'s [patch](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/overriding-dependencies.html) feature to override the address length locally (probably the quickest short term solution)
- Use a fork of Diem with our preferred address length (least preferred solution)

title: [Discussion] What is the authoritative state of a fastx system?
body:
Today @stella3d asked a very important question, that is also at the heart of a lot of the client side issue, namely: **What is the authoritative state of a fastx system?** 

We have potentially many authorities storing different objects at different versions, and having processed different certificates. What should a block explorer display? There are a few levels at which we can answer this question:

View 1. The state of the fastx system is the causal execution of the set of all certificates that can be retrieved from all authorities. In this view a replica of the system simply downloads and re-executes as many certificates as it can from authorities, and considers this the state of the system. Interesting, once we reason in terms of certificates, there are no forks or no need to rollback -- all certificates (subject to the safety assumption of the system) are correct and can be executed in any causal order to yield correct versions of the overall database.

View 2 (more strict). The state of the fastx system is the causal execution set of all certificates that can be retrieved from any >2/3 authorities. In this definition we consider a certificate to be within the state of the system if it has been shared and executed with at least >2/3 authorities, and therefore is guaranteed to be available if we ask any >2/3 authorities. This is in line with the reconfiguration logic as we are thinking about it today. 

The short coming with Def 1 was that a certificate in the hand of 1 dishonest authority may not be guaranteed to be available. However, in all cases a certificate that is used by another certificate (through the objects created) is guaranteed to satisfy Def 2. So if one sees a certificate they know that all certificates that came before it will definitely be part of the state even if we use the more strict definition 2. But how can we ensure, as a replica, that a certificate we got from say a single authority, will also have been seen by >2/3 other authorities? There are three options: (a) we ask them if they have seen it, (b) we give it to them directly or indirectly (through a gossip sync) or (c) we see the objects resulting from the execution of the cert being used in the execution of a subsequent cert.

Is fastx really that different from other blockchains. Yes, and no, in my opinion. It is not different in the sense that different authorities have a different view of the state. Blockchains based on byzantine consensus (cosmos) also have authorities that are consistent but may have seen up to a different sequence of the stream of transactions. Proof of work chains are even worse in that there may be forks for a while, while the longest/most work chain is not the same for all. 

However, what is different about fastx is that two consistent states cannot be compared in terms of the length of the sequence of transactions executed (as in BFT), or the hash of the last block (as in Pow). Instead if two authorities A1 and A2 in fast

title: [crash recovery] recover from loss of liveness
body:
### Description
When a loss of liveness happens (ex at least `f + 1` nodes crash) then the cluster doesn't seem able to recover and make progress. The nodes that are crashing when booted again they are not able to make new proposals and nodes are not able to advance in rounds. More specifically the following scenario describes the issue:

We assume a `cluster of 4 nodes` in total `(f = 1)`. We are testing the behaviour by shutting down at the same time `2 of them (f+1)`.

Before we shutdown the nodes I can see that all of them have produced and exchanged the certificates in round 7 and stored them. Now:
* I shutdown 2 nodes (let’s call them crashed nodes)
* The 2 healthy nodes are still creating their header proposals - for round 8 - and broadcast. Of course they receive votes only from each other since only those 2 are alive. They stop there and don’t make progress
* Then I bring up the crashed nodes
* The crashed nodes now receive the headers of round 8 (since the authors are retrying) that the healthy nodes made, and they vote
* The certificates from the healthy nodes for round 8 are produced (2 in total)
* Crashed nodes see the produced certificates of round 8 and set as their next round in proposer to be 7 (as part of [this](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/pull/465)). Although the crashed nodes have already the certificates for round 7 in their storage, those are not getting repopulated hence the proposer is empty - so no proposals can be made
* Cluster can’t progress further

### Steps to reproduce
The test here [TBC] perfectly describes the tests to reproduce and the current behaviour.

### Root cause
The root cause appears to be the proposer and the fact that the latest parents are not re-populated from disk for the nodes that have been crashed. We are already aware that we are lacking of crash recover mechanisms but this is something we want to resolve as part of them.

It has to pointed out that even if the https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/pull/465 was not introduced the crashed nodes wouldn't be able to make progress as they would start their proposals from round 1. However, because the nodes[ are not re-voting](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/c953fc6e633fcbfa5fd6b70da75ca18cf4562869/primary/src/core.rs#L269) for rounds that already voted from proposals of other nodes, the crashed node would never be able to make progress and propose a certificate as not enough votes would be received.

title: [narwhal] recover from loss of liveness - last header missed
body:
## Steps to Reproduce Issue

On a 4 validator cluster we let the rounds advance and then we shutdown the 2 out of 4 nodes (f+1 failures). The protocol should stop and no round should advance.

The 2 nodes that crashed although they did receive the headers that the other 2 healthy nodes made, and acknowledged (network) the receipt of the headers, they crash and they never manage to vote for them.

We bring one of the crashed nodes up. The crashed node manages to make a proposal but it doesn't vote for any of the last sent headers that it previously missed.

## Expected Result

Since the restarted node had previously acked on the receipt of the header, it should vote for it after the restart. That would allow the corresponding certificates getting created and eventually have a quorum of certificates available for round advancement.

## Actual Result

The restarted node doesn't vote for the acked header after restart. That leads to the 2 healthy nodes that proposed their headers to never able to create the corresponding certificates - as not enough votes are gathered. Cluster stalls as not enough certificates are produced (quorum) in order for the round to advance.

title: [fastx] How to facilitate Bulk Sync between authorities, authorities and full replicas
body: Authorities need re-assurance at some point they have ingested all updates from other authorities up to a point. Similarly, full replicas (ie. nodes that try to replicate all state, but do not validate yet) also need to track the full state of the system, and to do so need to know they have received all updates from authorities up to a point. This design task is about designing this mechanism.

title: SUI; BLOCKCHAIN; JAVASCRIPT
[consensus] Replace DFS by a BFS
body:
- the consensus collects blocks which commit is implied by the commit of a scion, as a DFS from that descendant node,
- as a consequence, blocks reported to be committed are not in order of their rounds (which reflects the order in which they've been proposed),

https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/32e4abc336b370a832472e8d12ad29d28a255185/consensus/src/lib.rs#L310-L356

While not incorrect, this is sub-optimal, as blocks should get committed in proposal order.
Moreover, in so far as we'd use the same API for a mempool to list commit-able blocks (called "collections" in a mempool context), this should be a shared BFS routine over the block DAG.

Details:
The BFS, will report the nodes in the ancestry by order of generational rank (parents, grand-parents, great-grand-parents, ...), whereas we at the moment use a DFS, which favors the lineage of the first parent of the node, over the second, third, and so on.
Since the reporting order is correlated with the commit order when Narwhal reports to a downstream consensus, that first parent lineage stands a better chance to be committed faster than others, and can this front-run those other lineages.

title: [Umbrella] [Sync] Engineering plan for follower (A), transaction dissemination (B) and check pointing (C)
body:
This issue gathers the tasks road map following the extensive design discussions in #194 . We we develop particular components we will make individual issues to discuss, but here we present the big picture. 

Priority A: A client / authority / replica can request historic and real time local transaction sequence from another authority.

* [x] Implement authority local sequence and client request for historic and current transactions sequence.  
* [x] Implement client side requests for historic local sequence and real-time live sequence updates. (#636 & #1048 @laura-makdah )

Priority B: Authorities proactively share certificates (and optionally transactions) with each other, to ensure honest authorities are close to having processed the same set of certificates. ( @laura-makdah & @gdanezis )

* [x] Leverage facilities in Priority A to implement a variant of the Murmur protocol (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.01738.pdf) between authorities. In that protocol each authority initiates following O(LogN) others (bidirectonally) at random, and exchanges their list of local updates. 
* [x] Allow authorities that follow each other to maintain a diff of their databases.
* [ ] Extend the protocol to allow an authority to request a non-real time sequence from another authority, and to create a diff between its local state and the state of the remote authority.

Priority C: Protocols to leverage the information available on authorities to derive periodic checkpoints where a super-majority of authorities agree to the set of certificates processed up to these points.

* [x] Create a DB to store information about the checkpoints, index transactions by checkpoint, and maintain sets of local transactions that are not yet included in the checkpoint, as well as sets of transactions in checkpoints not locally processed. (@gdanezis )
* [x] Create logic to leverage the local transaction diffs in Priority B, and a consensus mechanism to define global checkpoints, following the spanning tree checkpointing concepts (see https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1TSs1FPC9INZMpipP1vP2dK7XMmOXtHk5CLWFKO6s7p8/edit?usp=sharing) initially. (@gdanezis )
* [ ] Connect the information about the global sequence to the local sequence to facilitate local sequence sync in Priority B.
* [x] Connect  to a consensus mechanism to actually construct the checkpoint (@asonnino ), and process incoming checkpoints from agreement.

cc: @LefKok who can provide reviews on design & feedback on interactions with reconfig. @kchalkias who will want to review crypto.

title: Checkpoint process can stall if all fragments sent to consensus are lost
body:
Currently when we generate new fragment we send it to consensus and do not have any persistent retry mechanism. After we generate fragment for each authority, we simply assume that those fragments are persisted in consensus and never try to generate new fragments again. We have an in-memory retry in `CheckpointConsensusAdapter`, but it is not persistent.

Sending to consensus itself is not persistent/reliable - there are multiple places where fragments in flight to consensus are buffered in memory(namely the consensus sending channel on the SUI and batch buffering on narwhal) and will be lost when node restarts.

To be more specific the problematic flow is this - we generate fragment for each authority, persist them in `local_fragments` table and send them to consensus. If node soon fails before submitting consensus batch, `local_fragments` will contains fragments for all validators and checkpoint process will be permanently stalled for the validator - no new fragment can be generated(since there are pending fragments persisted in DB) and pending fragments in `local_fragments` will never make into consensus(since they were sent to channel but lost due to node restart).

title: Poison pill TX can cause infinite crash loop
body:
In devnet, we encountered a poison-pill tx, which caused validators to panic.

The retry log worked as designed, and gave up after 3 retries:

```
2023-01-14T18:16:04.111982271Z stderr F 2023-01-14T18:16:04.111940Z ERROR sui_core::authority: Abandoning in-progress TX after 3 retries.
```

However, the execution driver continued attempting to execute the cert:

```
2023-01-14T18:16:04.112126242Z stderr F 2023-01-14T18:16:04.112077Z DEBUG sui_core::execution_driver: Pending certificate execution activated. digest=7jqRiFm5XoFhRHwPKQwyeaYESwYJsfWdXpqYfwBkGGFw
```

We need to make sure this can't happen. Possible solutions:
- Probably the easiest method: Maintain a permanent record of txns that have exceeded the retry count, and check that in execution driver. We should also guard against automated resubmission of the tx. Lastly, we'll need a tool to remove the poison tx from this list once we have patched the bug. 
- Alternative: Add crash detection to execution driver. We can't use drop handlers becuase we use `panic = abort`, but we could have execution driver mark txns as in progress, and then mark them as finished when they either succeed or fail - any tx that is marked in progress when we load it from the table was in progress during a crash. However it doesn't follow that it was the tx that caused the crash.

body:
Sui's consensus mechanism fall's under the category of PoSA(Proof of Staked Authority) rather than how it's termed now D-PoS(Delegated-Proof of stake) 

Proof of Staked Authority (PoSA) is a combination of Delegated Proof-of-Stake (DPoS) and Proof-of-Authority (PoA) consensus mechanisms. 

Holders of Sui token decide on the validator their Sui token needs to be delegated to (D-PoS) but this validator set is a confined one in the Sui blockchain as only approved and Identity verified individuals can be a validator also termed as 'Authorities' in the docs.

Henceforth the assertion to Hybrid Consensus mechanism of PoSA

title: [authority] Add safe concept of time
body:
Use-cases we care about such atomic swaps, auctions, tokens with an unlock delay, breeding cooldown period, etc. require time. Here is a the proposed design for exposing time to transactions:

- (#6056) Expose the creation timestamp in signed header data coming back from consensus.  Only headers with timestamps in the past can be signed.
- Expose the creation timestamp within Move by introducing a `Clock` type, and an API: `tx_context::time(clock: &Clock, ctx: &TxContext): u64` that fetches the creation unix timestamp from the header associated with the response from consensus that ordered the transaction being run.
  - The only way to gain access to the `Clock` type is to request it as a parameter in an entry function.  It cannot be stored,  or duplicated.
  - This parameter is not supplied by the caller, instead it is supplied by the SDK for calls that request it as an entry function parameter.
  - To make this clear, `Clock` parameters can only appear at most once, by reference, immediately preceding the context parameter.  An entry function with a non-conforming signature will fail to verify.



## Forcing a transaction through consensus
The existence of a `&Clock` entry function parameter signals that the transaction must **go through consensus** as that is the only way time can be passed in.  This means that a transaction that otherwise involves only owned objects will go through consensus if it needs access to time.

Initially, the plan is to introduce `Clock` as a shared object at a well-known address which **SDKs must supply for you**.  The main upside to this approach is that it is quick to get up and running and adds no special cases, but it requires special SDK support, and all transactions that require time will be sequenced against the same object, which could lead to contention, hurting throughput.  In future we may consider one of the following strategies:

- Move the responsibility of supplying the `Clock` to the validator, which will recognise the type and force the transaction into consensus, but also supply it in the move adapter layer.
- Implement sharding by supplying a number of `Clock` objects and having SDKs spread the load between them.
- Implement read-write locks for shared objects, so that reads on the `Clock` do not introduce data dependencies between each other.

title: [process_header] fetch parents when processing header after remove_collections
body:
### Description
When using Narwhal with an external consensus the user has the ability to remove certificates via the `remove_collections` call.
When calling the `remove_collections` call we are truncating all the related data from various stores `certificates_store, header_store, payload_store etc`. The issue here https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/issues/230 describes a problem that could arise by that and the corresponding solution that has been applied can be found [here](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/pull/451).

However, we are still suffering by the same issue when processing a new header proposal that points to parents of previous round (which certificates we have effectively deleted). That makes the [checking of parents](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/afb331ff289d876524207f7a58ac0f3aa9ac8a01/primary/src/core.rs#L221) effectively never get fulfilled as the parent certificates have been already deleted by all the nodes stores.
 
### Steps to reproduce
* Spin up a cluster of nodes
* Let the cluster advance a bit
* Perform a read_causal and traverse all the certificates
* Remove all the certificates via the `remove_certificates` call
* Now no new header proposal can be processed. Each node should endlessly try to fetch the header's parents.

### Possible solution
We could probably apply the same solution as we have done in https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/pull/451 and use the DAG. There are a couple of impediments to do so though:
1. The [get_parents](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/afb331ff289d876524207f7a58ac0f3aa9ac8a01/primary/src/core.rs#L221) call of the synchronizer is supposed to return the actual certificates 
2. The above is needed because checks need to be made to confirm that (a) the parents are strictly of the previous round (b) there is enough support by the parents (a stake of `quorum` is required)

To be honest I don't see many different solutions to this that doesn't involve keeping around - at least for some period - enough certificates that will allow the node to successfully process and vote on new headers. A few ideas involve:
1. Always keep the certificates of round >= `gc_round` _in memory_ and defer to those to fetch the parents.  Since [this PR](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/pull/378) we have linked the `remove_collections` with the existing GC mechanism. If anything this can probably speed up even the normal processing, as under normal circumstances we will always fetch parents of the previous round (near cache data). 
2. Alternative to (1) we can just keep only the parents _of the previous round_ in memory. 
3. Keeping the `round` and `origin` info in the DAG when the certificate gets dropped. It will definitely increase the expected in memory size but it will still allow us to by pass this issue
4. Keep the above info in a side rocksdb storage

title: Sui On-Chain Randomness Update Mechanism not Documented
body:
Thanks for the great work, sui team!

I've read the doc about [sui on-chain randomness](https://docs.sui.io/guides/developer/advanced/randomness-onchain), and found the related [code](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/16624f1dfa12f4afbf4c37eff40219b28dd1916b/crates/sui-framework/packages/sui-framework/sources/random.move#L90-L121), but it's not clearly stated how the randomness is updated, like in what scenarios or frequency etc. 

Why it's concerning to me is that it's related to how safely I can rely on the randomness. For example, attackers may predict the number if they call for the random number in a time window very close to mine, just because epoch/randomness_round were not updated timely, considering sui::random uses global randomness state.

Please update the doc for this. Thanks!

title: Shared Object Deletion
body:
### Deleting Shared objects

This feature will allow shared objects to be deleted whereas previously, only single owner objects had the ability to be deleted. This will allow the storage rebate to be claimed for unused shared objects. The storage rebate will be given to entity that submits the transaction that successfully deletes the shared object. 

In order to delete a shared object, we will have the ability to define an entry function that takes the shared object in by value. From within this function, authorization logic can be added to define who can delete the object, and under what circumstances it can be deleted. For example, the function which deletes a certain shared object may also take as input a designated single owner object whose possession allows the given user the ability to call the deletion function. 

Alternatively, a shared object may have the ability to be deleted by any user, but only after a specific attribute on the object itself has been added or meets a certain requirement. For example, a shared object might have a field that records the last updated time, or last accessed time. The deletion function can then check for a certain duration of inactivity on the object before allowing deletion. 

If multiple transactions were submitted concurrently that both delete and mutate a given shared object, the execution order of these transactions will be decided by consensus, and if a mutation was sequenced after the deletion, the transaction that mutates the previously deleted object will fail execution. The default base gas fee will be charged for this failed transaction in line with the standard pricing of transactions that fail execution.

### Implications for existing objects

If there is a module that defines an object type, and some of the instances of this type are shared, while some instances are owned, there may already be functions defined that take this object by value. Currently, if a transaction calls such a function with a shared object input, there will be a runtime error. After this feature is introduced, shared objects will also be allowed as input objects by value, so no runtime error will occur. This would now allow deletion of those shared objects if such logic was currently written in an existing function that deletes that input object. Besides this particular instance of object types that have both shared and owned instances and functions implemented that delete the owned instances, no changes to existing behavior will occur. 

### Limitations

While shared object will now have the ability to be deleted in the standard way, ie calling `object::delete(id)` they will not have the ability to be deleted via wrapping or to be transferred to a single owner. If we were to define a function that takes a shared object S as input by value and does something like `Wrapper { id: object::new(context), S }` this would case a runtime error, likewise if we were to attempt to transfer this object to a single

title: Need to ensure all sequenced shared object transactions are included in last checkpoint of epoch
body:
There are two problems that need to be solved:
1. Stop sequencing transactions at a specific checkpoint. To be able to do this, we need to change our checkpoint construction point. Basically whenever a new fragment is received from consensus, we would need to try to build the checkpoint, and if it succeeds, we stop accepting new messages from there for as long as the validator is halted. This allows us stop sequencing precisely at the checkpoint C - 1.
2. Then we need to be able to block wait all transactions that have been sequenced but not executed before checkpoint C. To do this we would need to try to execute all transactions in pending_transactions that are shared object transactions bypassing validator halt.

title: Redesign Node & spawn_primary
body:
Currently when we want to spawn a new primary node we are using the [spawn_primary](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/d76c440d4aaef15fb3f490aeb160bcf922c9d21f/node/src/lib.rs#L102) method which is a static function that receives a bunch of inputs and returns a vector of JoinHandles of the spawned tasks. This method is suffering from a few issues
1. **The input is becoming quite convoluted** as more and more inputs are passed in
2. **When we need to communicate information out of the Primary node**, a channel needs to passed in (ex see `tx_confirmation`) which is used in a top to bottom approach penetrating several components until is finally used
3. Our nodes can be used with internal or external consensus. Some inputs apply only when one mode is being used (ex the `tx_confirmation`, `execution_state`) which creates unnecessary setup in the opposite case and makes things unclear on what's needed or not

Because of the above its becoming quite hard to extend and manage the primary node especially in case (2). For example, if I would like to receive the `last_committed_round` outside of the primary node, the way to do it , it would be to create a new channel and pass it as part of the `spawn_primary` continue growing the method inputs and add additional complexity by again passing down the channel until it is being used by the necessary component (ex in this case it would be the [state_handler](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/main/primary/src/state_handler.rs)).

### Proposal

To tackle the above we could probably refactor the [Node](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/d76c440d4aaef15fb3f490aeb160bcf922c9d21f/node/src/lib.rs#L95) and the `spawn_primary` method. Ideally we would like to return back something like a handle (ex like we do in [Dag](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/d76c440d4aaef15fb3f490aeb160bcf922c9d21f/consensus/src/dag.rs#L363) or in [MockBlockSynchronizer](https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/d76c440d4aaef15fb3f490aeb160bcf922c9d21f/primary/src/block_synchronizer/mock.rs#L173)). Then we can use this handle to do several stuff like:
1. `subscribe` (or listener) to receive supported outputs (ex committed certificates, latest committed round etc)
2. `manage the node` , like it shutdown

title: [timestamp MVP] Add a timestamp to Narwhal blocks
body:
### Description of the simplest thing that could possibly work

We would like to add a basic timestamp to the Narwhal block header (in the context of an external consensus, "Narwhal collection headers").

The simplest approach would be recursive, using the parents of the block itself: each block has 2f+1 parents, which each themselves have a timestamp, and taking the median of these is necessarily a value within the interval of honest timestamps ([the median has a breakdown point of 50%, and a 2f+1 sample is majority-honest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robust_statistics#Breakdown_point)).

One simple approach would be to ask the validators to produce a timestamp on header minting that is greater than the median of their parents. 

The timestamp would be considered correct, and voted on, as part of header verification, if the time stamp is not more than 15s in the future by the time it arrives at validators.

## Synchronicity

[The requirement of 15s is derived from Ethereum practice](https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/2227589f9b4baea159fb0ef4db385b252f4093d9/consensus/ethash/consensus.go#L268-L276). It's got a lot of mileage and should not pose practical problems. Note that a key to not introducing any synchronicity assumptions is that the block should *not* be rejected if it is > 15s in the future. Instead, it should be "parked" for later examination (at a time where it's no longer >15s in the future).

Since every block proposal has a round, and those rounds advance once the voter has received 2f+1 certificates, the "shelf" of blocks with a timestamp too high to be voted on should be cleared:
- either through re-examinations,
- or when the round advances,
whichever comes first.

## Modifications 

The header creation is here:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/2572c24b034a447a0b23e5df08843d733e868b09/primary/src/proposer.rs#L82-L105

It should integrate a timestamp creation.

The header verification is here:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/2572c24b034a447a0b23e5df08843d733e868b09/types/src/primary.rs#L149-L173

It should integrate timestamp verification as indicated above, and gate voting on the header by returning a sentinel error (aka a rust `Error` enum with an appropriate variant) to this caller:
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/2572c24b034a447a0b23e5df08843d733e868b09/primary/src/core.rs#L384-L388

This should change the return type of `verify` to return that sentinel error.

For remediation, we can take inspiration for the "temporary shelving and re-execution" pattern we have implemented for the block synchronizer (when we're trying to import a certificate and don't yet have all its parents):
https://github.com/MystenLabs/narwhal/blob/410ed5d51b7bd2a1e67fd8b2960986c39be58da9/primary/src/synchronizer.rs#L50

## Side-effect

Since this interacts with local time, it becomes a core performance issue that the node has an accurate local time in the first place. We s

title: TransactionEffects V2
body:
Overview

TransactionEffects is one of the core data types in Sui. It contains information that summarizes the execution result of a transaction. The current version v1 is defined in https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/main/crates/sui-types/src/effects/effects_v1.rs. This type is evolved overtime and many fields are added to adapt new features introduced in the system. However these newly added fields lack of consistent design, which creates many problems. In this design we will propose TransactionEffectsV2, which has a coherent semantics around object changes, and will bring many benefits to the rest of the system.

## Problems with `TransactionEffectsV1` ### 1. The semantics of effects are very confusing and hard to reason about. Fields in effects data type are added individually without coherent design with each other. It becomes very difficult to reason about the semantics when we we look at them together. Very few people fully understand the precise semantics of each field in the effects related to objects. This is very problematic given how fundamental this data structure is. It also makes it very difficult to build any downstream component that depends on the semantics effects (e.g. state accumulator, object pruner and etc.). A few example questions to demonstrate the complexity of the fields: - If an object is wrapped right after creation in the same transaction, will it show up in `created` or `wrapped`? - If an object is deleted right after creation in the same transaction, will it show up in `created` or `deleted`? - Will `deleted` / `wrapped` objects show up in `modified_at_versions`? - Will `unwrapped` / `unwrapped_then_deleted` objects show up in `modified_at_versions`? Overall, too much semantics are put in the effects that make it difficult to reason about and extend. We need to keep effects simple and only include primitive results around objects. ### 2. Dealing with effects is not efficient and often require unnecessary object store reads When producing effects as well as consuming effects in various places, we often always have to read the object store again, which is quite inefficient and adds to I/O pressure: - When we finish executing a transaction, in order to generate effects, we [[consult](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/main/sui-execution/latest/sui-adapter/src/programmable_transactions/context.rs#L743)](https://github.com/MystenLabs/sui/blob/main/sui-execution/latest/sui-adapter/src/programmable_transactions/context.rs#L743) the object store for each object that’s not in the input (which relies on whether an object exists as wrapped tombstone). - In state accumulator, for each modified objects in each effects, we have to read the object store to get its old digest. ### 3.
